segments.title: The stop and the contract
sections: The Stop That Cost More Than You Planned

cues.text: You know the moment. The level was right, the stop, the resting order that ends the trade when price goes against you, was where the structure said it should be, and the loss was bigger than the number in your head.
Price did not gap. You sized the trade on a feeling about a few points, on a contract whose points you had never priced.
Every risk decision on this site is in R, your base risk per trade. The platform does not take R. It takes contracts, and it fills in ticks.
The space between those two units is where a planned 1R loss quietly becomes 2.5R. This module closes that space.
It works mechanically, with MNQ, the Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 future, as the example and MES, the Micro E-mini S&P 500 future, beside it.
Now, the contract. When you buy one MNQ you do not buy a share of anything. You enter an agreement whose value is set by a formula.
The Nasdaq-100 index, multiplied by a fixed dollar amount. For MNQ that amount is two dollars. For MES it is five dollars, on the S&P 500.
That amount is the contract multiplier. It is also the point value: what one full index point is worth on one contract.
Every point the index moves, one MNQ changes by two dollars and one MES by five, in your favour or against you.

Nothing is ever delivered. The rulebook says it in six words: Delivery shall be by cash settlement. At expiry, the day the contract ends, it is closed out against a final index price, and the difference is paid in cash.
No truck pulls up with a Nasdaq. That is what cash settlement means.
The rule: before you trade any futures contract, know what it is a multiple of, and by how much.
Getting it wrong is carrying one contract's arithmetic onto another: two products on the same index, or two indexes that look alike on a chart.
It reveals that you are reading the chart, not the instrument. The fix is a card beside your screen with five lines. The first is the contract unit and its point value.

segments.title: Ticks, points and the three steps
sections: Ticks, Points And What They Are Worth

cues.text: Price does not move smoothly. It moves in fixed steps, and the exchange sets the step.
That step is the tick. For MNQ and MES it is a quarter of an index point, so one point is four ticks.
Tick value is what one tick is worth on one contract: tick size times the multiplier.
For MNQ, a quarter times two dollars is fifty cents a tick. For MES, a quarter times five dollars is a dollar and a quarter.
The two contracts share a ruler. They do not share a bill.
Now, the conversion. Three steps, in this order, every time.
One: points to ticks. Stop distance in points, divided by tick size. On MNQ and MES, points times four.
Two: ticks to risk per contract. Stop ticks times tick value.
Three: contracts. Your base R divided by the risk per contract, rounded down.
As one line: contracts equals R divided by stop ticks times tick value.
Rounding is always down. Two and a half contracts is two, never three. Rounding up is a small, silent rise in risk on every trade.
Other contracts follow the same three steps. Only tick size and tick value change, and they change more than you would expect.
MYM, the micro Dow, ticks a full point.
M2K, the micro Russell 2000, ticks a tenth of a point.
Micro gold and micro euro are deliverable: a position held into expiry ends in delivery, not cash.
Read the spec page, the exchange's specification sheet for the contract you trade. Never carry another contract's numbers onto it.
The rule: size comes from R and stop ticks, through the tick value. The order is your level, the zone you marked; then stop, risk, size, entry.
Getting it wrong is picking the size first, three contracts every trade, and letting it set the risk. Or setting a loss and squeezing the stop until it fits.
It reveals the size was chosen before the structure was read. The fix: write the stop in ticks before the size, with the arithmetic beside it. A size with no arithmetic is not a plan yet.

cues.text: Index futures trade nearly around the clock: Sunday 6 p.m. to Friday 5 p.m. Eastern, with a daily halt from 5 to 6 p.m.
CME publishes in Central time. This course writes every time in Eastern.
RTH, regular trading hours, is 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, the US cash stock session. ETH, extended hours, is the rest.
Where does a day end? CME's day starts at the evening open: Tuesday begins Monday at 6 p.m. Eastern.
This course ends the day at 4 p.m. Eastern, the cash close. A convention the framework chooses, not a market fact.

Two reasons. The levels you mark for your next session, the prices you plan to trade from, come from the cash session. And the daily settlement, the exchange's official closing price, falls in the last thirty seconds before 4 p.m.
Your platform may define the prior day differently. Neither is wrong; know which you are looking at.
The rule: every time on your plan is in Eastern, and your day ends at 4 p.m. Eastern.
Getting it wrong is a Central time read as Eastern. The fix: end your chart's session template at 4 p.m. Eastern, and write the hours on the card as line three.
Now, settlement in full. The daily settlement uses the lead month, the contract expected to be most active.
MNQ and MES are listed quarterly: March, June, September and December. Each month is its own contract.
The final settlement is set once, at expiry, from the opening prices of the index stocks on the third Friday. Trading in the expiring month stops at 9:30 a.m. Eastern that day.
The roll is moving from the expiring month to the next: your charts, your levels, and any position you keep.
Most traders move before the last morning, so the expiring contract thins out. The customary roll date is the Monday before the third Friday.
The roll date is published in advance. It is the one date here that sends an invitation.
The rule: know the expiry date and your roll date for the contract you trade, before the week they fall in.
Getting it wrong is an order sent to the expiring month. The fix: the roll date is line five on the card, and in roll week you read the contract month on the ticket before your first order.

cues.text: Margin is the deposit your broker requires before it lets you hold a contract. It is not a price, and it is not the most you can lose.
Initial margin opens the position. Maintenance margin is the lower level your account must stay above to keep it.
Leverage in one line. At an index level of 20,000, one MNQ is 40,000 dollars of exposure, and a loss is measured against all of it, not against the margin.
Brokers change margin when they choose, so this module quotes no figure. CME's margin pages and your broker's page have the live numbers.
R decides size. Margin only caps it. The rule: size from R and stop ticks; margin is a ceiling, never a target.
Getting it wrong is thinking the margin covers six, so six. It reveals the broker's permission is being read as advice.
Margin will happily let you trade six. Margin does not know where your stop is.
Now, funded and evaluation accounts: the same contract with four constraints written by the firm, not the exchange.
One: a daily loss limit, a loss that stops trading for the day.
Two: a drawdown limit, a loss from a reference balance that ends the account.
Three: allowed hours, the times positions must be flat.
Four: allowed contracts, which products and how many at once.
None of these change what a tick is worth. They change the room you have, and firms change their terms, so read your firm's own pages.

Evaluation accounts are simulated, and some funded accounts are too. A simulated fill is not a fill at the exchange, so those trades are tagged sim in your journal, the record of every trade, and never pooled with live trades.

The firm's limits are a backstop around your rules, not a replacement. Getting it wrong is trading up to the firm's limit instead of your own 2R kill switch, the daily loss limit from Module 2, or counting a passed evaluation as evidence.

Tax, in one paragraph. In the US, regulated futures like MNQ and MES are generally Section 1256 contracts, taxed as 60 percent long-term and 40 percent short-term, and a position still open at year end is treated as sold that day.
That is a fact about the tax code, not tax advice. Check with a tax professional.

segments.title: Worked case: one R on two contracts
sections: Worked Case: One R On Two Contracts

cues.text: A composite plan, built to show the arithmetic. It belongs to no one, it uses invented numbers, and it stops before any outcome. This is a hypothetical illustration, not actual trading.
Risk per trade is 1R. The numbers are chosen because they divide easily, not as a recommendation. Module 14 covers choosing yours.
The structure puts the stop 80 ticks away, 20 points. The same 80 ticks is used on both contracts, so only the arithmetic changes.
On MNQ, 80 ticks at the MNQ tick value puts 0.4R on each contract.
One R divided by 0.4R is two and a half, rounded down to 2 contracts, risking 0.8R. Rounding up to 3 would risk 1.2R.
On MES, the same 80 ticks puts a full 1R on each contract. One contract, risking exactly 1R.
Same R, different contracts: two MNQ or one MES on this stop. Neither is more aggressive. Each is 1R or under, and that is all the size line is for.
Now the structure is wider. The stop is 160 ticks. On MNQ each contract carries 0.8R, so the size is 1 contract.
On MES each contract would carry 2R, more than your whole risk for the trade. So the size is 0, and there is no MES trade here.
You do not raise R to make it fit. You do not squeeze the stop to make it fit. The arithmetic does not negotiate.
A wider stop cut the size on both contracts. It never raised the risk.
Check it against the 2R kill switch from Module 2. At the MNQ size, two losses come to 1.6R, inside it. On MES, two full losses reach 2R, and the switch fires.
The rule: size comes from three numbers you know before the session: your base R, the stop in ticks, and the tick value. No margin figure, no index level, no view on where price goes.
Getting it wrong is letting a size you like set the stop. The case ran the other way: stop first, size last.

segments.title: Your contract card
sections: Can You Read Your Contract Without Looking?

cues.text: Can you read your contract without looking? Answer five for the contract you trade, from memory, then check each against its spec page.
One: contract unit and point value.
Two: tick size and tick value.
Three: session hours, including the daily halt, in Eastern.
Four: settlement method, and when trading in the expiring month stops.
Five: your next roll date.
One point for each match. Five of five: you know your instrument. Three or four: the missing lines go on the card before your next session. Under three: no live order until all five are written down.
The rule: one line overrides the score. If you missed the tick value, you have been sizing without it, so treat the total as under three.
Four out of five with the tick value missing is a zero in a nice jacket.
Your assignment. Open your contract's spec page on CME's site and write those five lines on a card, copied from the page, not from memory.
Keep the card beside the screen. That is the whole assignment. No card, no order.
Getting it wrong is filling the card from memory and never checking it against the page.

Where it goes next. The whole module in one line: size is the result of R, stop ticks and tick value, and everything else, margin, the firm's limits, the contract's size, is a ceiling around that number.
The 2R kill switch from Module 2 is a figure in the account setting: 2 times your base R. The tick arithmetic here is how you check it against the trades you plan.
Module 6, What Counts As A Level, puts the 4 p.m. boundary to work on the levels themselves. Module 14, Trade Construction, covers choosing your base R and the full sizing step.
